title: An Ethic of Basic Probity
author: Aaron M. Renn
summary: Aaron Renn responds to Matthew Yglesias's essay on how readily American culture accepts deception, including the admission that defending overstated claims was a mistake. Renn argues that the answer is not to match opponents' dishonesty but to rebuild an ethic of basic probity, honesty and factual accuracy from the ground up. He explains why lying persists: it works and is rewarded, whereas a Protestant-inflected culture once punished it. Drawing on E. Digby Baltzell and the Profumo Affair, he describes a shifted hierarchy of sins in which being a known liar carries little cost. He adds that institutional go-along-to-get-along cowardice is as serious as outright fabrication, citing Peter Thiel on the scarcity of courage. His conclusion is that the fix is structural as well as personal and will need incentives and a genuinely moral vision. The digest also briefly covers evangelical formation and local government.
points: Dishonesty flourishes because it is rewarded, so restoring honesty requires systems that reward truth-telling and punish lying rather than appeals to enlightened self-interest alone.
The decline of a culture that treated liars as disgraced has changed society's hierarchy of sins, which Renn illustrates with Baltzell and the Profumo Affair.
Institutional leaders' habit of going along to get along is as damaging as spectacular frauds, because too few people will tell the truth when it is personally risky.
Renn argues that rebuilding probity is a structural as well as a personal moral task and that proceduralist fixes will not be enough.
In the meantime, readers can support leaders who model the pursuit of truth rather than trying to out-propagandise opponents.
quotes: Why do people, even those who occupy the top rungs of society’s key institutions, lie so much today? Because it works. Because it’s rewarded.
Societies that wish to overcome the toxic effects of rampant dishonesty have to establish systems that reward telling the truth and punish lying.

And the answer, to be clear, is not to say that the bad guys are so vicious and opportunistic that we need to beat them by any means necessary! It’s to try to rebuild an ethic of basic probity, honesty, and factual accuracy from the ground up.

Multitudinous cultural changes have undermined the structural underpinnings of a culture of honesty. That’s not to say everyone was honest in the past - far from it - but there was an era in which honesty was a social norm, and in which being found a liar might well suffer significant consequences.

I would say that while Elizabeth Holmes style whoppers are a problem in our society, equally or more seriously as bad is the extreme go-along-to-get-along mentality that has been adopted by so many of our institutional leaders.

I’m very much in agreement with Yglesias that we need to rebuild an ethic of probity. But this will require institutional and cultural incentives to encourage good behavior. It’s a structural as well as personal moral issue.
